data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a methodological rule of 'critical preference' rather than an inductive inference; it survives by redefining rational action as the selection of the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby minimizing known error without assuming future uniformity. The cost of accepting this is the abandonment of any claim to probable truth or predictive certainty, leaving action as a non-rational gamble guided only by the best available critical scrutiny.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent implicitly assigns a higher subjective probability of future success to the corroborated theory, the distinction collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'rational action' requires any expectation of future regularity beyond the logical status of the theory, the defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' of paralysis (inaction) is deemed irrational, then an inductive supplement becomes necessary despite Popper's prohibitions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'induction' (inferring future truth from past success) and 'corroboration' (a logical report of past test performance). By treating the preference rule as a procedural heuristic for error avoidance rather than a truth-tracking probability update, the agent avoids the uniformity of nature assumption. The agent acts on Theory A not because A is likely true tomorrow, but because A is the only theory not yet known to be false under conditions relevant to the action.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
